sentences.text: Cetiosaurus was a primitive herbivore that walked on four legs and possessed a long neck with a small head.
Unlike most sauropods, this animal had relatively long forelimbs that were equal in length to its hindlimbs.
Estimates suggest the creature reached a length of about 16 meters and weighed roughly 11 tons.
Its tail was shorter than that of many other sauropods, and its neck was also relatively short.
The skull is largely unknown, although a brain case may be represented by specimen OUMNH J13596.
Sir Richard Owen initially thought the animal had crocodilian characteristics and considered it a gigantic sea reptile rather than a dinosaur.
Cetiosaurus was the first sauropod dinosaur to be described from bones, with the name coined in 1842 by Sir Richard Owen.
Owen named the genus Cetiosaurus in 1841, one year before he coined the term Dinosauria.
The genus is known from three skeletons discovered by the Phillips family near Bletchingdon in 1868 and 1869.
John Whitaker Hulke named Cetiosaurus humerocristatus in 1874 based on a humerus found at Sandsfoot near Weymouth in Dorset.
The species C. oxoniensis is based on three more or less complete specimens discovered starting from 1868.
Paul considered Cetiosaurus a feeding generalist that ate at both low and medium-high levels, based on its moderately long neck and limb proportions.
C. oxoniensis was officially designated as the type species of the genus Cetiosaurus in 2014.
Paul Upchurch and John Martin determined in 2003 that Cetiosaurus hypoolithicus and Cetiosaurus epioolithicus were invalid because they were nomina nuda.
Cetiosaurus brachyurus, named by Owen in 1842, is considered a nomen dubium.
Cetiosaurus rigauxi, named by Sauvage in 1874, is not a sauropod but a pliosaurid.
Cetiosaurus lived during the Middle Jurassic period between 171 and 165 million years ago in what is now Britain and possibly France.
Cetiosaurus oxoniensis is the best-known species from the Middle Jurassic.
Vertebrae of a related species were found in the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight.
It was determined in 1849 that some bones previously assigned to Cetiosaurus actually belonged to Iguanodontidae rather than sauropods.
It is debated whether Cetiosaurus humerocristatus is a valid taxon, as it is often considered a nomen dubium.
It is debated whether Cetiosaurus brevis should be the type species, as this would cause taxonomic instability with the genus Pelorosaurus.
It is debated why the dinosaurs of the London-Brabant Massif did not experience insular dwarfism despite the island's size.
Fossil tracks discovered in Oxfordshire in 1997 and 2024 are suggested to be Cetiosaurus footprints, though they could also belong to a diplodocoid.
